faq.q: Where does a tree make new wood?
faq.a: In the cambium, a thin living layer just under the bark. Each growing season it makes new wood on its inside and new inner bark on its outside.

faq.q: Why are tree rings light and dark?
faq.a: Spring wood grows fast, with big cells, and looks pale. Late summer wood grows slowly, with small, thick-walled cells, and looks dark. Together they make one year.
asks: What makes the lines in wood?

faq.q: How do you count tree rings?
faq.a: Count the dark bands from the centre out to the bark; each marks the end of one year. Scientists usually take a thin core with a hollow drill instead of cutting the tree down.
asks: How can you tell how old a tree is?

faq.q: What can tree rings tell us about the past?
faq.a: Ring widths record each year's growing weather, and scars show past fires. By matching ring patterns between living and dead trees, scientists have built records going back thousands of years.
Often not clear ones. Where it is warm and wet all year, trees grow steadily, so many show faint rings or none. Clear rings form where there is a cold or dry season.
asks: Do all trees have growth rings?

facts: Some Great Basin bristlecone pines in California are more than 4,800 years old, counted from their rings.
The study of tree rings is called dendrochronology.
Tree rings form clearly only where trees have a growing season and a resting season each year.

quiz.say: A tree stump shows 40 dark bands. About how old was the tree?
quiz.show: A tree stump shows 40 dark bands. About how old was the tree?
quiz.why: Each year adds one pale band and one dark band, so 40 dark bands means about 40 years.

wrong.1: Each dark band is a whole year, not half a year.
wrong.2: Counting both pale and dark bands as years would double the age.
